## Load Data

```{r load-data}
setwd("~/Downloads") 
load("youth_data.Rdata")
ls()
youth_data <- df
str(youth_data)
summary(youth_data)
```
# Binary Classification (Marijuana Use)
**Research Question:** Can high levels of emotional stress and poor parental communication predict whether a youth has ever used marijuana?
```{r}
# STEP 1: Data Cleaning and Feature Selection
# We want to model whether a youth has ever used marijuana (binary classification).
# We filter to only valid Yes/No responses (coded as 1 or 2).
# Predictors include emotional stress and parental monitoring, which are known behavioral influences.
# We convert demographic variables to factors to ensure categorical handling during modeling.
binary_df <- youth_data %>%
  filter(PRMJEVR2 %in% c(1, 2), !is.na(TALKPROB), !is.na(PRALDLY2)) %>%
  mutate(
    marijuana_use = factor(PRMJEVR2, levels = c(2, 1), labels = c("No", "Yes")),
    SEX = factor(IRSEX),  # Sex is a key demographic predictor
    RACE = factor(NEWRACE2),  # Race might correlate with cultural/social access
    parental_monitoring = factor(PRALDLY2),  # Parental monitoring as a behavioral signal
    stress_level = TALKPROB  # Emotional stress measured from youth responses
  ) %>%
  select(marijuana_use, stress_level, parental_monitoring, SEX, RACE, INCOME)
glimpse(binary_df)


# STEP 2: Train-Test Split
# We split the data into 70% training and 30% testing to evaluate model generalizability.
# Stratified sampling (via createDataPartition) ensures that class proportions (Yes/No) remain consistent.
set.seed(123)
trainIndex <- createDataPartition(binary_df$marijuana_use, p = 0.7, list = FALSE)
train_bin <- na.omit(binary_df[trainIndex, ])
test_bin <- na.omit(binary_df[-trainIndex, ])

# STEP 3: Decision Tree
# Decision trees help us understand what rules define marijuana use.
# We use method="class" to specify it's a classification problem.
# This baseline model reveals early predictors and structure of the data.
tree_bin <- rpart(marijuana_use ~ ., data = train_bin, method = "class")
rpart.plot(tree_bin, extra = 104) # Visualizes split structure with label annotations

# STEP 4: Random Forest
# Random forests improve over single trees by combining many (bagging).
# It handles noise, nonlinearities, and interaction effects better.
# We use ntree=100 for a stable ensemble size without excessive compute time.
rf_bin <- randomForest(marijuana_use ~ ., data = train_bin, ntree = 100)
varImpPlot(rf_bin)# Shows which variables are most influential across all trees

# STEP 5: Gradient Boosting (Binary Classification)
# Boosting builds trees sequentially, focusing on examples misclassified by prior models.
# We use the "bernoulli" distribution for binary classification.
# We set n.trees high (1000) with small learning rate (shrinkage = 0.01) to avoid overfitting.
# interaction.depth = 3 allows up to 3-way feature combinations.
# 5-fold cross-validation ensures we stop training at optimal point.
gbm_bin <- gbm(as.numeric(marijuana_use) - 1 ~ ., 
               data = train_bin,
               distribution = "bernoulli", 
               n.trees = 1000, 
               shrinkage = 0.01, 
               interaction.depth = 3,
               cv.folds = 5)
# Use CV to get the best tree count — prevents overfitting
best_iter <- gbm.perf(gbm_bin, method = "cv")

# STEP 6: Prediction and Evaluation
# Predict marijuana use using the best GBM model
# We evaluate results using confusion matrix (accuracy, precision, recall)
# ROC and AUC help us understand the model's ability to separate classes
pred_gbm_prob <- predict(gbm_bin, test_bin, n.trees = best_iter, type = "response")
pred_gbm <- ifelse(pred_gbm_prob > 0.5, "Yes", "No") %>% factor(levels = c("No", "Yes"))
confusionMatrix(pred_gbm, test_bin$marijuana_use)
roc_curve <- roc(test_bin$marijuana_use, pred_gbm_prob)
auc(roc_curve)
```

# Multi-Class Classification (Cigarette Use Frequency)
**Research Question:** How frequently do teens from different household and parental support backgrounds use cigarettes?**
```{r}
# STEP 1: Data Cleaning and Feature Structuring
# We are predicting how frequently youth use cigarettes (ordinal multi-class).
# We filter out rows with invalid or missing frequency data and convert our target to an ordered factor,
# since the classes (1–7) represent increasing usage frequency.
multi_df <- youth_data %>%
  filter(IRCIGFM %in% 1:7, !is.na(PRALDLY2), !is.na(IRCIGAGE)) %>%
  mutate(
    cig_freq = factor(IRCIGFM, ordered = TRUE),  # Ordered factor preserves ordinal structure
    parental_monitoring = factor(PRALDLY2),  # Key behavioral control feature
    first_use_age = IRCIGAGE,  # Early exposure may correlate with higher frequency
    SEX = factor(IRSEX),
    RACE = factor(NEWRACE2)
  ) %>%
  select(cig_freq, parental_monitoring, first_use_age, SEX, RACE, INCOME)
glimpse(multi_df)


# STEP 2: Train-Test Split
# Class stratification isn’t supported directly for ordered factors, but we aim for random balance.
# Missing values are omitted to prevent model errors.
set.seed(42)
train_idx <- createDataPartition(multi_df$cig_freq, p = 0.7, list = FALSE)
train_multi <- na.omit(multi_df[train_idx, ])
test_multi <- na.omit(multi_df[-train_idx, ])

# STEP 3: Decision Tree for Ordinal Classification
# rpart with method="class" creates a baseline tree.
# Though it treats output as nominal, it's useful for visualizing simple splitting logic.
multi_tree <- rpart(cig_freq ~ ., data = train_multi, method = "class")
rpart.plot(multi_tree, extra = 104)
pred_multi_tree <- predict(multi_tree, test_multi, type = "class")
confusionMatrix(pred_multi_tree, test_multi$cig_freq)

# STEP 4: Random Forest
# Builds an ensemble of trees to better capture interaction effects.
# Can handle noisy multi-class data better, though it treats the target as unordered.
multi_rf <- randomForest(cig_freq ~ ., data = train_multi, ntree = 100)
pred_multi_rf <- predict(multi_rf, test_multi)
confusionMatrix(pred_multi_rf, test_multi$cig_freq)
varImpPlot(multi_rf) # Identifies most important predictors across forest
# Use training set summary to check class counts
print(table(train_multi$cig_freq))

# STEP 5: Gradient Boosting (Multinomial)
# We switch to a multinomial distribution to handle multi-class target.
# Interaction depth and shrinkage are tuned low to minimize overfitting in rare classes.
multi_gbm <- gbm(as.numeric(cig_freq) ~ ., 
                 data = train_multi,
                 distribution = "multinomial", 
                 n.trees = 100,
                 interaction.depth = 2,
                 shrinkage = 0.05,
                 n.minobsinnode = 5,
                 bag.fraction = 0.5)


# STEP 6: Prediction and Evaluation
# We extract the class with the highest predicted probability for each row.
# Accuracy is assessed via confusion matrix, although imbalance may dominate.
gbm_class_preds <- predict(multi_gbm, test_multi, n.trees = 100, type = "response")
gbm_class_labels <- colnames(gbm_class_preds)[apply(gbm_class_preds, 1, which.max)]
gbm_class_labels <- factor(gbm_class_labels, levels = levels(multi_df$cig_freq))
confusionMatrix(gbm_class_labels, test_multi$cig_freq)
```

# Regression (Alcohol Use Days per Year)
**Research Question:** Can peer influence predict the number of days alcohol was consumed in the past year?
```{r}
# STEP 1: Data Cleaning and Feature Setup
# We aim to predict the number of days alcohol was consumed in the past year — a numeric target.
# Outliers (values >= 365) are removed to improve model reliability.
reg_df <- youth_data %>%
  filter(IRALCFY < 365, !is.na(IRALCFY), !is.na(PRALDLY2), !is.na(IRSEX), !is.na(NEWRACE2)) %>%
  mutate(
    alcohol_days = IRALCFY,
    parental_monitoring = factor(PRALDLY2),
    SEX = factor(IRSEX),
    RACE = factor(NEWRACE2)
  ) %>%
  select(alcohol_days, parental_monitoring, SEX, RACE, INCOME)
glimpse(reg_df)

# STEP 2: Train-Test Split
# We divide the data for regression modeling and remove any rows with missing values.
set.seed(101)
train_idx_reg <- createDataPartition(reg_df$alcohol_days, p = 0.7, list = FALSE)
train_reg <- na.omit(reg_df[train_idx_reg, ])
test_reg <- na.omit(reg_df[-train_idx_reg, ])


# STEP 3: Regression Tree
# rpart with method="anova" is used for numeric regression trees.
# This model gives a basic understanding of how features split based on continuous outcomes.
tree_reg <- rpart(alcohol_days ~ ., data = train_reg, method = "anova")
rpart.plot(tree_reg, extra = 101)
pred_tree_reg <- predict(tree_reg, test_reg)
postResample(pred_tree_reg, test_reg$alcohol_days)
# STEP 4: Random Forest (Regression)
# Random forest smooths out predictions across trees, reducing variance.
# It handles non-linear relationships and noisy data well.
rf_reg <- randomForest(alcohol_days ~ ., data = train_reg, ntree = 100)
pred_rf_reg <- predict(rf_reg, test_reg)
postResample(pred_rf_reg, test_reg$alcohol_days)
varImpPlot(rf_reg)

# STEP 5: Gradient Boosting (Gaussian)
# We use gaussian distribution because our target is continuous.
# Parameters are chosen to slowly learn patterns, avoiding overfitting.
# Cross-validation helps determine when to stop boosting.
gbm_reg <- gbm(alcohol_days ~ ., 
               data = train_reg,
               distribution = "gaussian",
               n.trees = 1000,
               shrinkage = 0.01,
               interaction.depth = 3,
               cv.folds = 5)

# STEP 6: Prediction and Model Performance
# Predict using best number of trees found via CV
# Evaluate using RMSE and R-squared to measure fit quality
best_iter_reg <- gbm.perf(gbm_reg, method = "cv")
pred_gbm_reg <- predict(gbm_reg, test_reg, n.trees = best_iter_reg)
postResample(pred_gbm_reg, test_reg$alcohol_days)
```
